# Introduction

Environmental burdens such as air pollution are inequitably distributed, with disparities often rooted in economic and social structures. Here, I investigate the extent to which demographics and socioeconomic status correspond with higher levels of air pollution in Los Angeles County, California.

# Setup

Before we get started, we must first install and load all necessary dependencies. Since this analysis uses R and Python at different stages, ensuring that both run smoothly in a Quarto document involves some additional setup.

# Get Data

## Demographic & Socioeconomic Data

Census tract-level demographic and socioeconomic data for Los Angeles County is sourced from the U.S. Census Bureau's 2018-2022 American Community Survey. Socioeconomic variables include the estimated number of residents living below the poverty line, income per capita, median household income, median home value, and percentage of college graduates per census tract. Demographic variables comprise the number of residents who identify as white, black, Asian, and/or Hispanic. These racial and ethnic categories were selected since they represented the largest demographic categories in Los Angeles County [@demograp2024]. Further details on the variables used can be found [here](https://api.census.gov/data/2022/acs/acs1/spp/variables.html).

To access the data, we require a U.S. Census API key which can be obtained [here](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html).

```{r}
# Configure API key (if needed)
if (Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") == "") { 
  census_api_key <- read_lines(here("api-keys/census-api-key.txt"))
  census_api_key(census_api_key, install = TRUE)
}

# Cache shapefiles for future use
options(tigris_use_cache = TRUE)
```

Once our API key is configured, we can query the data using the `{tidycensus}` package [@walker2024].

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Define variables
vars <- c(
  total_pop = "B01003_001E",            # total population                 
  white = "B02001_002E",                # white population     
  black = "B02001_003E",                # black population     
  asian = "B02001_005E",                # Asian population     
  hispanic = "B03002_012E",             # Hispanic population         
  poverty_status = "B17001_002E",       # population below poverty line              
  median_house_income = "B19013_001E",  # median household income                    
  income_per_cap = "B19301_001E",       # income per capita               
  median_value = "B25077_001E",         # median home value             
  pct_college = "DP02_0068P"            # percentage with college degree          
)

# Load data
la_county <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = vars,
  year = 2022,
  state = "CA",
  county = "Los Angeles",
  geometry = TRUE,
  output = "wide"
  ) |> 
  clean_names() |> 
  select(-ends_with("m")) |> # drop margin of error columns
  rename_with(~str_remove(.x, "_e$")) |> # drop "_e" from end of variable names
  filter(!geoid %in% c("06037599000", "06037599100")) |> # remove islands (Catalina & San Clemente)
  relocate(geometry, .after = everything()) |> 
  st_as_sf() # convert from tibble to data.frame to avoid issues with the row names in the predictions

# Save data
st_write(la_county, here("data/census/los-angeles-census-tracts.shp"), 
         append = FALSE, quiet = TRUE)
```

We use the resulting geodata to determine the appropriate bounding box for Los Angeles County which will be used to download air quality data in the next step.

```{r}
# Create bounding box
bbox <- la_county |> st_bbox() |> as.list() |> as.data.frame()

# Save bounding box
write_csv(bbox, here("data/output/los-angeles-bbox.csv")) 

print(bbox)
```

## Air Pollution Data

Nitrogen Dioxide ($NO^2$) is often produced by industrial activities and motor vehicle exhaust, with high concentrations being linked to respiratory problems [@whymeas]. As such, this analysis uses the average tropospheric $NO_2$ column density (mol/m²) as a proxy for air pollution. Note that this is a satellite measure of the whole air column, not a ground-level concentration in ppm. $NO^2$ data from July 2023 is sourced from the European Space Agency's (ESA) Sentinel-5P satellite [@sentinel].

Before we can download the data, we must first configure our credentials for the Sentinel Hub through the [Copernicus Data Space Ecosystem](https://shapps.dataspace.copernicus.eu/dashboard/#/).

```{python}
# Load credentials from environment variables (SH_CLIENT_ID, SH_CLIENT_SECRET)
sentinel_client_id = os.environ["SH_CLIENT_ID"]
sentinel_client_secret = os.environ["SH_CLIENT_SECRET"]
    
# Configure Sentinel Hub Python profile
config = SHConfig()
config.sh_client_id = sentinel_client_id
config.sh_client_secret = sentinel_client_secret 
config.sh_base_url = "https://sh.dataspace.copernicus.eu"
config.sh_token_url = "https://identity.dataspace.copernicus.eu/auth/realms/CDSE/protocol/openid-connect/token"
```

Once our credentials are configured, we define the key parameters such as the bounding box and resolution level for our API query. Note that the Sentinel Hub limits the number of pixels returned by each query, so we have selected a level of resolution (expressed in degrees) that maximizes resolution given this constraint.

```{python}
# Load bounding box area
bbox_df = pd.read_csv("../data/output/los-angeles-bbox.csv")

# Extract bounding box coordinates
bbox_row = bbox_df.iloc[0] 
coordinates = [bbox_row['xmin'], bbox_row['ymin'], bbox_row['xmax'], bbox_row['ymax']]

# Create a BBox object
bbox = BBox(bbox=coordinates, crs=CRS.WGS84)

# Resolution in degrees
resolution_degrees = 0.005

# Bounding box coordinates in WGS 84
xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = coordinates

# Calculate width and height in degrees
width_deg = xmax - xmin
height_deg = ymax - ymin

# Convert size from degrees to "pixels" (units at the given resolution)
width_px = int(width_deg / resolution_degrees)
height_px = int(height_deg / resolution_degrees)
```

We must also define an evalscript which specifies how the pixels are to be processed [@documenta]. Here, we take the average $NO^2$ for each pixel during July 2023.

```{python}
# Define eval script
evalscript_raw = """
//VERSION=3
function setup() {
  return {
    // This specifies the bands that are looked at
    // "dataMask" tells us whether or not there is data for a given tile
    input: ["NO2", "dataMask"],
    output: {
      bands: 1,
      sampleType: "FLOAT32" // data type to be returned
    },
    mosaicking: "ORBIT" // Will take all tiles over the specified period into account
    };
}

function isClear(sample) {
  return sample.dataMask == 1;
}

function sum(array) {
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    sum += array[i].NO2;
    }
  return sum;
}

function evaluatePixel(samples) {
  // Calculate mean of each pixel
  const clearTs = samples.filter(isClear)
  const mean = sum(clearTs) / clearTs.length
  return [mean]
}
"""
```

Next, we construct our query using the evalscript and key parameters. Since the Sentinel Hub restricts the amount of data which can be freely downloaded each month, this process is only performed if the data has not already been downloaded.

```{python}
# Get data if not already downloaded
if not os.path.exists("../data/copernicus/response.tiff"):
  # Formulate API query
  data_5p = DataCollection.SENTINEL5P.define_from("5p", service_url=config.sh_base_url)
  
  request_raw = SentinelHubRequest(
    evalscript=evalscript_raw,
    input_data=[
        SentinelHubRequest.input_data(
            data_collection=data_5p,
            time_interval=("2023-07-01", "2023-07-31"), # July 2023
        )
    ],
    responses=[SentinelHubRequest.output_response("default", MimeType.TIFF)],
    bbox=bbox,
    size=(width_px, height_px),
    config=config,
    data_folder="../data/copernicus/"
    )
    
  # API request
  raw_data = request_raw.get_data(save_data=True)
```

# Combine Data

Next, both spatial datasets are combined and the average $NO_2$ column density (mol/m²) is calculated for each census tract. We use the coordinate reference system of the raster data in order to preserve its quality as best as possible.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Load pollution data
air_qual <- rast(here("data/copernicus/response.tiff"))
names(air_qual) <- "avg_air_qual" # rename layer

# Load US census data 
la_county <- st_read(here("data/census/los-angeles-census-tracts.shp"))

# Align vector data CRS with raster data CRS
la_county <- st_transform(la_county, crs = st_crs(air_qual))

# Calculate average air quality (NO2 column density, mol/m2) by neighborhood
avg_air_qual <- extract(air_qual, la_county, fun = mean, na.rm = TRUE) 

# Append average air quality to vector data
la_county$avg_air_qual <- avg_air_qual$avg_air_qual

df_with_na <- la_county |>
  rename( # restore variable names
    "total_pop" =  "totl_pp", 
    "hispanic" = "hispanc",
    "poverty_status" = "pvrty_s",
    "median_household_income" = "mdn_hs_",
    "income_per_cap" = "incm_p_",
    "median_home_value" = "medn_vl",
    "pct_college" = "pct_cll"
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    pop_density = as.numeric(set_units(total_pop / st_area(geometry), "1/km2")),
    pct_white = white / total_pop,
    pct_black = black / total_pop,
    pct_asian = asian / total_pop,
    pct_hispanic = hispanic / total_pop,
    poverty_rate = poverty_status / total_pop
  ) |>
  select(-total_pop, -white, -black, -asian, -hispanic, -poverty_status) |>
  relocate(c(avg_air_qual, geometry), .after = everything())

# Remove observations with missing data
df <- df_with_na |> 
  na.omit()

# Add IDs to rows
row.names(df) <- df$geoid
```

Several patterns emerge when we map our socioeconomic variables. Higher levels of median household income, median home value, and percentage of residents with college degrees are more prevalent in southwest Los Angeles County. Perhaps unsurprisingly, the census tracts with the highest income per capita appear to be located in and around Beverly Hills and Bel-Air. Additionally, above average poverty rates appear to be concentrated in south Los Angeles and in the northeast of Los Angeles County. While not a socioeconomic variable, population density is fairly low throughout most census tracts with the exception of the areas in and around Downtown Los Angeles.

# Analysis

Before proceeding with our analysis, we check for multicollinearity among the independent variables that we intend to include in our model.

```{r}
# Calculate correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- df |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(-geoid, -name, -avg_air_qual) |>
  cor()

# Format table
kable(cor_matrix, format = "html", title = "Correlation Matrix") |> 
  kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) |> 
  scroll_box(width = "100%", height = "500px")
```

To prevent multicollinearity from potentially impacting our models, we remove variables with pair-wise correlations above 0.65. The remaining socioeconomic variables include `median_home_value` and `poverty_rate` and the remaining demographic variables include `pct_white`, `pct_black`, `pct_asian`, and `pct_hispanic`. Additionally, `pop_density` is included since it may represent another driver of air pollution.

```{r}
multicol_vars <- findCorrelation(cor_matrix, cutoff = 0.65)
include_vars <- colnames(cor_matrix)[-multicol_vars]
print(include_vars)
```

## Develop Baseline Model

Next, we use linear regression to model the relationship between socioeconomic as well as demographic variables and air pollution. This model does not take spatial information into account and will serve as our baseline model.

```{r}
# Initial regression model to serve as baseline
ind_vars <- paste0(include_vars, collapse = " + ")
formula <- as.formula(glue("avg_air_qual ~ {ind_vars}"))
linear_model <- lm(formula = formula, data = df)
summary(linear_model) 
```

## Spatial Autocorrelation

To determine whether the model's performance depends on geography, we perform a Moran's $I$ test to check for autocorrelation in the residuals. Spatial weights for neighbors are obtained by applying inverse distance weighting to the 100-nearest neighbors for each census tract.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Get centroids
centroid_coords <- st_centroid(df)

# Create list of neighbors
neighbors_list <- knn2nb(knearneigh(centroid_coords, k = 100)) # 100-nearest neighbors

# Get distance for all spatial neighbor links
dists <- nbdists(neighbors_list, centroid_coords)

# Compute inverted distances
p <- 2
epsilon <- 0.0001
inverted_dists <- lapply(dists, function(x){1/(x^p + epsilon)})

# Get spatial weights for neighbours lists
wts <- nb2listw(neighbors_list, glist = inverted_dists, style = "B") # inverse distance weights

# Use Moran's I test to see if there is still autocorrelation in our residuals
moran.test(linear_model$residuals, wts)
```

The Moran’s $I$ test statistic is moderately strong and positive (0.72) and is statistically significant (p-value \< 0.001). Therefore, it is appropriate to use models that can account for spatial autocorrelation.

```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
# Get residuals and lagged residuals
residuals_linear_model <- residuals(linear_model)
lagged_residuals_linear_model <- lag.listw(wts, residuals_linear_model)
res <- data.frame("lagged_residuals" = lagged_residuals_linear_model, "residuals" = residuals_linear_model)

# Plot residuals vs. lagged residuals
ggplot(res, aes(x = residuals, y = lagged_residuals)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_number(), breaks = breaks_pretty()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(), breaks = breaks_pretty()) + 
  labs(
    x = "Residuals",
    y = "Lagged residuals"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Spatial Regression

### Spatially lagged X model

The spatially lagged X model produces coefficient estimates for both the covariates and lagged covariates.

```{r}
slx_model <- lmSLX(formula, data = df, listw = wts, zero.policy = TRUE)
summary(slx_model)
```

Furthermore, the spatially lagged X model allows us to decompose these coefficient estimates into their direct and indirect impacts.

```{r}
# Look at direct and indirect impacts
summary(impacts(slx_model))
```

To test whether the spatially lagged X model accounts for autocorrelation in the residuals, we once again perform the Moran’s $I$ test.

```{r}
moran.test(slx_model$residuals, wts)
```

Surprisingly, Moran’s $I$ is greater with the spatially lagged X model than the linear regression model (0.73 vs. 0.72). Moreover, the model still demonstrates significant autocorrelation, leading us to believe that the spatially lagged X model does not sufficiently capture the spatial dependence present in the data.

### Spatial error model

The spatial error model includes a spatial lag in the model's error term in order to capture latent spatial processes that are not already accounted for in the model estimation and, as a result, appear in the model's residuals.

```{r}
error_model <- errorsarlm(
  formula = formula,
  data = df,
  listw = wts
)
summary(error_model, Nagelkerke = TRUE)
```

Once again, we apply the Moran's $I$ test to check for persistent autocorrelation in the residuals.

```{r}
moran.test(error_model$residuals, wts)
```

Notably, Moran's $I$ is still moderately strong and positive (0.47), however the observed value is substantially lower than the estimates obtained using the other models.

## Evaluate Model Fit

We evaluate the fit of our models using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC).

```{r}
aic_results <- AIC(linear_model, slx_model, error_model)

kable(aic_results, format = "html", caption = "AIC Comparisons for Models") |>
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"))
```

Given that the spatial error model receives the lowest AIC, we consider it to be the model of best fit.

# Discussion

The spatial error model is assessed to be the model of best fit. This model estimates a positive and statistically significant relationship between air pollution and median home values (p-value \< 0.001), population density (p-value \< 0.001), the share of black residents (p-value \< 0.01), the share of Asian residents (p-value \< 0.001), and the share of Hispanic residents (p-value \< 0.001). A negative and statistically significant relationship between air pollution and poverty rate also exists at a significance level of $\alpha$ = 0.05 (p-value \< 0.05). Finally, the model did not find a statistically significant relationship between air pollution and the share of white residents (p-value = 0.324).

The significant positive $\lambda$ value (0.029, p-value \< 0.001) confirms the presence of spatial autocorrelation, justifying the use of a spatial model over a standard linear regression model. Furthermore, a Nagelkerke pseudo-$R^2$ value of 0.65 suggests that the model explains a substantial portion of the variance in air quality. These findings reveal significant correlations between socioeconomic as well as demographic factors and air pollution levels across Los Angeles County, underscoring the interconnected nature of social inequities and environmental hazards.

This analysis has several limitations. First, the context is specific to Los Angeles County, with further research required to determine whether similar patterns exist in other major U.S. metropolitan areas. With the exception of population density, the models used in this analysis rely solely on socioeconomic and demographic variables. It does not take other factors that may contribute to air pollution into consideration such as traffic patterns. Furthermore, we use $NO_2$ column density as a proxy for air pollution when it may be appropriate to examine other types of air pollution measures, including some combination of different measures. Additionally, this analysis only compares the performance of three types of models, namely linear regression, spatially lagged X linear regression, and spatial error regression. Future work could test the performance of more complex spatial models. It is also worth noting that $NO^2$ appears to be highly concentrated in areas near Downtown Los Angeles. As such, it may be appropriate to include a variable in the model that represents the distance between the center point of a given census tract from Downtown Los Angeles since this may explain a substantial portion of differences in air quality.

Future research should aim to validate these relationships and explore the mechanisms driving these associations, including the potential role of urban planning, industrial activity, and transportation patterns. Additionally, longitudinal studies could examine how these relationships evolve over time, especially in the context of policy interventions and urban development.
